files.lesson.md: --- order: 12 unit: sci9 node: AC9M9M02 n3 uses: [AC9M9M02 n1, AC9M9M02 n2] assumes: [AC9M8N02 n1, AC9M8N02 n2, AC9M9A01 n1, AC9M9A01 n2] connection: microgram-dose title: Real measurements summary: "Prefixes are powers of 10, so converting units is multiplying or dividing by a power of 10. A slip of a thousand is a real error." language: maths voice: { name: af_heart, speed: 1.1 } hook: "A label says 250 micrograms. A note says 0.25 milligrams. Same dose, or not?" app: command: node "$REPO_ROOT/tools/serve.mjs" "$REPO_ROOT/dist/_playground-board" 8349 url: http://127.0.0.1:8349/index.html readySelector: "#gsum" layout: full explainPicture: { ref: units.yml#explain-pic, caption: "$250$ micrograms is $2.5 \\times 10^{2}$ µg. A microgram is $10^{-3}$ mg, so it's $2.5 \\times 10^{-1} = 0.25$ mg." } explainClip: query: { code: "@units.yml#explain", fresh: 1, id: explain } caption: "Micrograms to milligrams: the power drops by 3" say: "A microgram is a thousandth of a milligram. The power drops by three." clip: - caption: { text: "250 µg = 2.5 × 10² µg.", say: "Two hundred fifty micrograms is two point five times ten squared." } - wait: 900 - caption: { text: "1 µg = 10⁻³ mg: the power drops by 3.", say: "One microgram is ten to the minus three milligrams." } - click: Make k smaller - click: Make k smaller - click: Make k smaller - wait: 900 - caption: { text: "2.5 × 10⁻¹ = 0.25 mg.", say: "Two point five times ten to the minus one is point two five milligrams." } - wait: 800 --- Prefixes like milli and micro are powers of 10. That makes converting units a job for scientific notation. ## Predict: label and note ```step stage: predict insight: "Committing to whether the two doses agree shows who sees that a milligram is a thousand micrograms, and who matches 250 with 0.25 by the digits." check: type: predict q: "A medicine label says the dose is 250 micrograms. A doctor's note says 0.25 milligrams. Are they the same dose?" options: - "Yes: they're the same" - "No: the label is 1000 times the note" - "No: the note is 1000 times the label" - "No: they're 100 times apart" actual: "Yes. A milligram is 1000 micrograms (10³ µg), so 0.25 mg = 0.25 × 1000 = 250 µg." ``` These are two ways to write one amount, or two different amounts. Which? ## Run: shift the point ```step stage: run insight: "Changing the unit changes the number by a power of 10, so converting moves the decimal point." try: { playground: board, starter: "units.yml#run", height: 600 } check: { type: board, text: "$0.25$ mg is $2.5 \\times 10^{-1}$ mg. A microgram is a thousandth of a milligram, so there are 1000 times as many micrograms. Set the board to $2.5 \\times 10^{2}$. Was your prediction right?", when: "a = 2.5 and k = 2" } ``` Try a few. A bigger power means a bigger number: that's what happens when you change to a smaller unit. ## Investigate: converting with powers ```step stage: investigate insight: "Divide the two powers of 10 to convert between units: milligrams to micrograms is 10⁻³ ÷ 10⁻⁶ = 10³. Dev multiplies the powers instead." tasks: - check: type: number q: "1 mg is $10^{-3}$ g and 1 µg is $10^{-6}$ g. So 1 mg = $10^{k}$ µg. What's $k$?" answer: 3 explain: "10⁻³ ÷ 10⁻⁶ = 10^(−3 − (−6)) = 10³: a milligram is 1000 micrograms." - check: type: bug code: "working.txt#dev" text: "Dev converts 0.25 mg to micrograms. Click the line where his working goes wrong." answer: 3 fault: logic misconception: prefix-convert-multiply explain: "Line 3: to find how many micrograms are in a milligram, divide: 10⁻³ ÷ 10⁻⁶ = 10³. So 0.25 mg = 0.25 × 10³ = 250 µg." - check: type: question q: "Which is the biggest?" options: ["$5 \\times 10^{-3}$ g", "$5 \\times 10^{-6}$ g", "$5 \\times 10^{-9}$ g"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "5 × 10⁻⁶ is a thousand times smaller than 5 × 10⁻³.", "5 × 10⁻⁹ is the smallest."] explain: "All have the number part 5, so compare the powers: −3 is the biggest." ``` ### Divide the powers Here's a conversion the other way, from micrograms to milligrams. ```worked 250 \text{ µg} :: The label. 2.5 \times 10^{2} \text{ µg} :: In scientific notation. 1 \text{ µg} = 10^{-3} \text{ mg} :: A microgram is a thousandth of a milligram. 2.5 \times 10^{2} \times 10^{-3} :: Multiply by the power of 10. 2.5 \times 10^{-1} \text{ mg} = 0.25 \text{ mg} :: Add the powers: 2 + (−3) = −1. ``` Now try one on paper: a tablet is 0.5 mg. How many micrograms is that? Write it as $5 \times 10^{k}$ µg and type $k$. ### Find the mistake Read Dev's working. Should the powers be multiplied or divided? ### Which is the biggest? ## Modify: change the units ```step stage: modify insight: "One change at a time: millimetres to nanometres, a made-up measurement from metres, and a ratio of two sizes." try: { playground: board, starter: "units.yml#vary", height: 620 } tasks: - hint: ["A millimetre is 10⁻³ m and a nanometre is 10⁻⁹ m.", "10⁻³ ÷ 10⁻⁹."] check: { type: number, q: "$3$ mm is $3 \\times 10^{k}$ nm. What's $k$?", answer: 6, explain: "1 mm = 10⁻³ ÷ 10⁻⁹ = 10⁶ nm, so 3 mm = 3 × 10⁶ nm." } smaller: check: { type: "number", q: "Just the powers: what's $-3 - (-9)$?", answer: 6, explain: "−3 + 9 = 6." } - hint: ["A nanometre is 10⁻⁹ m.", "Divide: 1.2 × 10⁻⁷ by 10⁻⁹."] check: { type: number, q: "A particle is $1.2 \\times 10^{-7}$ m wide. How wide is it in nanometres?", answer: 120, explain: "1.2 × 10⁻⁷ ÷ 10⁻⁹ = 1.2 × 10² = 120 nm." } - hint: ["Divide the number parts.", "Subtract the powers."] check: { type: number, q: "Edge case: how many cells of width $5 \\times 10^{-7}$ m fit across a grain $2.5 \\times 10^{-3}$ m wide?", answer: 5000, explain: "2.5 ÷ 5 = 0.5 and −3 − (−7) = 4: 0.5 × 10⁴ = 5000." } ``` ### Millimetres to nanometres ### Metres to nanometres ### How many fit? ## Practise: convert ```step stage: practise insight: "Converting between prefixes both ways, mixed; the review keeps multiplying fresh." tasks: - check: type: number q: "$2$ mg is $2 \\times 10^{k}$ µg. What's $k$?" answer: 3 explain: "1 mg = 10³ µg." - check: type: number q: "$5 \\times 10^{-9}$ m is $5 \\times 10^{k}$ mm. What's $k$?" answer: -6 explain: "1 nm = 10⁻⁹ ÷ 10⁻³ = 10⁻⁶ mm." smaller: check: { type: "number", q: "Just the powers: what's $-9 - (-3)$?", answer: -6, explain: "−9 + 3 = −6." } - check: type: answer q: "$4.2 \\times 10^{-3}$ g is how many milligrams?" answer: "4.2" form: simplified feedback: - ["4200", "A gram is the bigger unit: 1 g = 1000 mg. 4.2 × 10⁻³ × 10³ = 4.2."] explain: "4.2 × 10⁻³ g × 1000 mg/g = 4.2 mg." - check: type: number q: "Review: work out $(2 \\times 10^{3}) \\times (4 \\times 10^{4})$ as $8 \\times 10^{k}$. What's $k$?" answer: 7 explain: "2 × 4 = 8 and 3 + 4 = 7." ``` ### Bigger to smaller ### Smaller to bigger ### Decimal answer ### Review Multiplying, from the last lesson. ## Make: back to the label ```step stage: make insight: "Coming back to the label: the same dose written two ways, and what a slip of 1000 would do." tasks: - hint: ["Convert 0.25 mg to micrograms.", "Then compare 250 mg with 250 µg."] check: type: reasoning paper: true q: "The label says 250 micrograms. Someone reads it as 250 milligrams. How many times too much is that?" steps: - ["$1 \\text{ mg} = 10^{3} \\text{ µg}$", "a milligram is 1000 micrograms"] - ["$250 \\text{ mg} = 250 \\times 10^{3} \\text{ µg}$", "convert the milligrams to micrograms"] - ["$(250 \\times 10^{3}) \\div 250 = 10^{3}$", "compare with the real dose"] answer: "1000" answerLabel: "Times too much" feedback: - ["1", "1 mg is not the same as 1 µg. Convert both to the same unit."] - ["100", "A milligram is 1000 micrograms."] criteria: - "I converted both amounts to the same unit." - "I used 1 mg = 10³ µg." - "My answer is a power of 10." explain: "250 mg = 250 000 µg, which is 1000 times 250 µg." - check: type: question q: "A label says $0.5$ mg per tablet. Which is the same dose?" options: ["500 micrograms", "5 micrograms", "50 micrograms", "5000 micrograms"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "1 mg is 1000 µg, so 0.5 mg is 500 µg.", "1 mg is 1000 µg, so 0.5 mg is 500 µg.", "1 mg is 1000 µg, so 0.5 mg is 500 µg."] explain: "0.5 × 1000 = 500 µg." ``` ### Too much Back to the label. Work it out on paper first, then type your answer. ### Same dose Prefix sizes (milli 10⁻³, micro 10⁻⁶, nano 10⁻⁹): [SI prefixes, BIPM](https://www.bipm.org/en/measurement-units/si-prefixes). The doses here are made up for the task, not real prescriptions. **Also used in** - **Science and medicine.** Doses, lengths on a microscope and amounts in chemistry are all written with prefixes. - **Next.** Year 9 Real numbers: where scientific notation sits among the numbers. ```teacher summary: Students convert between unit prefixes by dividing powers of 10 and use scientific notation for very small and very large measurements, including a label and a note with the same dose written two ways (AC9M9M02, node 3). time: 40 timing: Predict and Run 8 min · Investigate 12 min · Modify 10 min · Practise and Make 10 min goals: - I can convert between prefixes using powers of 10. - I can compare measurements written in scientific notation. - I can say what a slip of 1000 means for a dose. struggle: "Which way to convert. Ask students: after the conversion, should the number be bigger or smaller?" before: > Do the Run board yourself first. Students need Calculating in scientific notation. The one idea: a prefix is a power of 10, so converting divides one power by the other. The common mistake is multiplying the powers (Dev's working). Prefixes are from the BIPM SI table. The doses are invented for the lesson; do not use them as real doses. running: - "Predict: take a show of hands. Those who chose 1000 times either way didn't convert the units first." - "Run: ask students whether the number should get bigger or smaller when the unit gets smaller." - "Paper: the try-one after the worked example and the 1000 times slip in Make are worked on paper first. Books out, and look for both amounts in the same unit." - "Modify: before 3 mm to nanometres, ask which unit is smaller." stuck: - see: A student gets 10⁻⁹ for milligrams to micrograms. ask: Did you multiply or divide the powers? fix: "Divide: 10⁻³ ÷ 10⁻⁶ = 10³." - see: A student says 0.25 mg is 25 µg. ask: How many micrograms in one milligram? fix: "1000: 0.25 × 1000 = 250." stretch: A nanometre is a billionth of a metre. How many nanometres fit across a 1 mm dot? support: "A ladder of prefixes: kilo, base, milli, micro, nano, with the power of 10 beside each." leads: | Finishes AC9M9M02. Where it leads: Year 10 growth and decay, science measurements. exit: q: How many micrograms are in 3 milligrams? a: 3000, or 3 × 10³. explain: > Prefixes are powers of 10: milli is $10^{-3}$, micro is $10^{-6}$, nano is $10^{-9}$. To convert, divide one power by the other. 1 mg $= 10^{-3} \div 10^{-6}$ µg $= 10^{3}$ µg, so 0.25 mg is 250 µg. ```

files.working.txt:
# Dev's working for the "find the mistake" task. Plain text: students click the wrong line, nothing runs.

# region: dev
Convert 0.25 mg to micrograms.
1 mg = 10⁻³ g and 1 µg = 10⁻⁶ g.
So 1 mg = 10⁻³ × 10⁻⁶ µg = 10⁻⁹ µg.
So 0.25 mg = 0.25 × 10⁻⁹ µg.
# endregion
